# Sarah Putnam
### For Alameda School Board
Every student deserves the opportunity to learn, participate, and succeed. As a student with an IEP, a disability-rights advocate, an early childhood educator, and an AUSD parent, I’ve learned how much access and support matter.Those experiences shaped ACCESS for AUSD, my framework for building equity and accessibility into the entire educational plan. We need to plan for every student from the start, instead of fixing problems one student, one school, or one complaint at a time.
### IN THE NEWS
Read news coverage, interviews, and endorsements from Sarah’s campaign.
EXPLORE THE COVERAGE →
ACCESS FOR AUSD
# A | Access for All
C | Comprehensive Planning
C | Centered on Each Student
E | Equity in Opportunity
S | Systemic Solutions
S | Success for All
DON'T HAVE KIDS IN AUSD? You still have a stake in our schools.
"If you're disappointed by your elected officials, grab a clipboard, get some signatures, and run for office yourself."
—Barack Obama
### Follow Your School Board
Board decisions affect students, parents and caregivers, educators, staff, and the use of public money. You should not have to hunt for the information you need to follow the Board’s work or make your voice heard.
Regular AUSD Board meetings are generally held on the second and fourth Tuesdays of the month.
Open session generally begins at 6:30 p.m.
City Hall Council Chambers, Third Floor
2263 Santa Clara Avenue
Alameda, CA 94501
A closed session may be scheduled earlier. Members of the public may attend and comment in person or remotely. Always check the official agenda for the final date, time, location, and participation instructions.
View Upcoming Agendas Attend or Comment Watch Live Watch Past Meetings Request Agenda Notices
Sarah’s campaign website is not the official source for Board meeting notices. Meeting dates and participation procedures may change. Please use the official AUSD agenda for the most current information.
## Principles & Priorities
### ACCESSIBLE SCHOOLS
A = ACCESS FOR ALL
Every student should be able to access their school, their education, and the opportunities available to their peers.
LEARN MORE →
### INDEPENDENT OVERSIGHT
C = COMPREHENSIVE PLANNING
Ask questions. Examine the evidence. Demand accountability.
LEARN MORE →
### IEPs, 504s & STUDENT SUPPORT
C = CENTERED ON EACH STUDENT
Students should receive the services, accommodations, and support they need without families having to fight for them.
LEARN MORE →
### FAMILIES & EDUCATORS DESERVE A VOICE
E = EQUITY IN OPPORTUNITY
Good decisions start by listening to the people who experience our schools every day.
LEARN MORE →
### RESPONSIBLE USE OF PUBLIC FUNDS
S = SUCCESS FOR ALL
Public dollars should be spent thoughtfully, transparently, and with students at the center of every decision.
LEARN MORE →
## Meet Sarah
WHY I’M RUNNINGEvery child deserves the chance to discover their potential. I’m running to keep our decisions about money, buildings, and student support focused on that promise. ACCESS for AUSD is how I would approach that work.
### Rooted in Alameda
Five generations of family roots, and my own years caring for children in this community.
Some of you know me as Sarah Hinkley, and others as Sarah Putnam. You may remember me as a preschool teacher, a nanny, a PTA member or a parent at Lum, Love, NEA, Maya Lin, Encinal and Alameda High or a student at the College of Alameda.
My family's roots in Alameda span five generations, beginning in 1910. But my connection to the community is not only something I inherited. Alameda families trusted me to care for their children, and I have watched many of them grow up, graduate, and go on to college.
### When Access Became Personal
My experiences as a student with an IEP, a wheelchair athlete, and a teenager facing inaccessible schools.
I navigated school with an IEP, and as a wheelchair athlete I learned independence, teamwork, and what it meant to be part of a community that expected disabled young people to participate fully.
But my experience in public school was very different. At 15, I became the named plaintiff and class representative in Putnam v. Oakland Unified School District, a federal disability-rights case challenging inaccessible schools.
This wasn't an abstract fight about accessibility. I was a high school student trying to get an education. I encountered bathrooms I couldn't use, cafeteria tables I couldn't access, classrooms I couldn't safely enter, and ramps that were inaccessible or hazardous. These weren't inconveniences. They affected where I could go to school, where I could learn, and whether I could participate alongside other students.
The accessibility barriers left me without a high school I could safely and fully attend. Instead of receiving an accessible high school program, I was provided only one hour of home instruction each day.
My disability wasn't preventing me from going to school. The barriers in my school were.
### A Fight Bigger Than One Student
What fighting for access taught me about planning ahead and holding systems accountable.
What began as my family's fight for my education became something much larger. The case represented students with physical disabilities across Oakland who were being denied equal access to their schools because of architectural barriers. At its heart was a simple idea: students with disabilities should have the same opportunity as their classmates to attend school, get to their classrooms, participate in programs, and be part of their school communities.
One lesson from that experience has stayed with me ever since: it should not be the student's job to discover every barrier and then fight to have it removed.
The court made that point in my case. Schools have a responsibility to identify accessibility problems and plan for access rather than waiting for a student or parent to complain.
That shaped how I think about public institutions today. Asking questions, planning ahead, and holding systems accountable isn't hostility. It's how we prevent families from having to fight problems that should have been addressed in the first place.
### From Student Advocate to Educator
What teaching and caring for young children taught me about meeting individual needs.
My commitment to children and education eventually became my profession. I studied Early Childhood Education extensively through the Peralta Colleges and worked as a Lead Preschool Teacher. I ran preschool classrooms, developed curriculum, and worked directly with young children at a critical stage in their development.
I also worked as a special needs nanny, where supporting a child often meant understanding that child's individual needs and finding approaches that worked for them. Those experiences reinforced something I had already learned from my own education: children do not all learn, communicate, or develop in the same way.
Early childhood education taught me how much happens before a child ever reaches kindergarten. Children are developing language, problem-solving skills, independence, relationships, emotional regulation, and the foundations they will build on throughout their education.
Teaching young children means observing closely, adapting when something isn't working, communicating with families, and meeting children where they are while helping them move forward.
### An AUSD Parent
From Scouting and PTA involvement to navigating IEPs and 504 Plans, I have spent years showing up for children.
Scouting has been part of my life since I was young. I was a Girl Scout through the Cadette level. Years later, I became a Boy Scout parent, helping with race-car projects and supporting my child as they worked toward merit badges.
Those experiences reinforced the value of service, hands-on learning, and adults showing up for young people. I brought that same involvement to my children's schools.
My family has been part of the Lum, Love, NEA, Maya Lin, Encinal and Alameda High communities. At Lum Elementary, I was heavily involved with the PTA and became part of a community of parents, teachers and staff working together for our school.
My experience as an AUSD parent has also included navigating the system for children with different needs. One of my children graduated from AUSD with an IEP, and another currently attends with a 504 Plan. I have attended meetings, worked with teachers and staff, and when problems couldn't be resolved at the school level, I have reached out to the district for help.
Sometimes that worked. People listened, followed through, and helped us find a solution. Other times, calls went unanswered or commitments to follow up didn't happen. I've experienced both sides of the system: what it looks like when it works for a family and what it feels like when a family has to keep pushing just to get an answer.
I've also learned that students who need support don't fit into one category. A student with an IEP or 504 Plan may be learning right alongside their classmates in a general education classroom. Sometimes what allows that student to participate and succeed is an accommodation, a service, a different approach, or simply having adults who recognize what that individual student needs.
I have seen what our schools can accomplish when those supports work. I have also seen how exhausting it can become for families when they don't.
Families shouldn't have to become experts in the system just to make the system work for their child.
### Why I Picked Up the Clipboard
I tried to resolve accessibility barriers through the existing system. When that failed, I decided to run.
This campaign began when one of my children needed a wheelchair for four months. I wanted my child to have the same opportunity as every other student: to enter school safely, attend class, and participate fully.
Instead, accessible routes sometimes led to locked gates. An intercom intended to provide assistance went unanswered. My child was repeatedly left waiting outside and was physically injured while navigating barriers I had raised with the school and district.
I made phone calls, requested the district's ADA plans, toured the campus, identified barriers, and asked who was responsible for accessibility. Too often, calls went unanswered and promised follow-up never came.
I later encountered another barrier at the renovated Kofman Auditorium, where I was told that wheelchair seating was available only at the back. It showed me that these problems were larger than one entrance, one building, or one student.
I had challenged a school district over disability access before. I never expected to find myself fighting again, this time as a parent trying to get my own child safely into school.
Families should not have to act like lawyers to secure basic access for their children. I stopped waiting for someone else to fix it. I picked up a clipboard and decided to run for School Board.
## Where I Stand
Not every School Board decision fits neatly into a list of priorities. Here’s how I would apply ACCESS for AUSD to some of the questions facing our schools and our community.
### LGBTQIA+ STUDENTS & COMMUNITY
A = ACCESS FOR ALL
Every student, family, and staff member deserves to be treated with dignity and respect. Our schools should be places where LGBTQIA+ people know they belong.
READ MY POSITION →
### CELL PHONES IN SCHOOLS
C = CENTERED ON EACH STUDENT
Teachers should not have to compete with phones for their students' attention. But keeping phones off and away shouldn't unnecessarily separate students from a means of communication during an emergency.
READ MY POSITION →
### PROTECTING NEIGHBORHOOD SCHOOLS
C = COMPREHENSIVE PLANNING
Our schools are part of the communities built around them. Before we talk about which schools to close, let's talk about what we need to do to keep them open.
READ MY POSITION →
### MUSIC & ARTS IN OUR SCHOOLS
E = EQUITY IN OPPORTUNITY
Arts education should be part of a complete education, and access should not depend on which AUSD school a student attends.
READ MY POSITION →
### AI & SCREENS IN OUR SCHOOLS
S = SYSTEMIC SOLUTIONS
This is the only childhood our children get. I support a moratorium on generative AI and an end to routine personal-screen use in classroom instruction. Before moving forward, AUSD must demonstrate educational benefit and explain how it will protect children’s learning and ability to think for themselves.
READ MY POSITION →
ACCOUNTABILITY IN ACTION
Good decisions start with listening, asking questions, and examining the evidence. Here’s where I’m putting ACCESS for AUSD into practice: looking closely at community concerns, following public dollars, and asking whether our schools are delivering for students. I’ll share what I learn and what still needs answers.
### WHEN COMPLIANCE IS NOT COMMITMENT
AUSD was required to address a documented racial disparity in how Black students were identified for certain disabilities. The public deserves to know what changed, whether outcomes improved, and who is accountable for continuing the work.
READ MORE →
### MUSIC & ARTS IN AUSD
A community concern raised questions about whether students across AUSD have equal access to music and arts education and how Proposition 28 funding is being used. We're gathering the data and asking the questions.
READ MORE →
### WHAT DID VOTERS ACTUALLY APPROVE?
AUSD described Measure E as renewing and consolidating two existing parcel taxes without raising the tax rate. But what did voters understand would remain the same, and what authority did they give future Boards to change spending priorities?
READ MORE →
### ENDORSED BY THE BAY AREA REPORTER
I’m honored to receive the Bay Area Reporter’s endorsement for Alameda Unified School District Board of Education, full term.

### INDEPENDENT OVERSIGHT
ACCESS for AUSD: C = Comprehensive Planning
### WHAT I BELIEVE
The School Board should do more than approve what is placed in front of it.
Board members are elected to provide independent oversight, ask hard questions, and make sure major decisions are supported by evidence.
### WHY IT MATTERS
Public trust must be earned.
When the public is being asked to trust major spending decisions, long-term projects, or changes that affect students and families, that trust has to be earned. Transparency means more than publishing documents. It means making sure the community can understand how decisions were reached, what assumptions were used, and whether the promised results were delivered.
### WHAT I WILL DO
I will ask hard questions and follow the evidence.
As a board member I will examine the evidence behind major decisions, follow up when answers are incomplete, and ask for independent review when the public deserves greater clarity. I will not assume that a recommendation is correct simply because it comes from inside the district.
ASK QUESTIONS. MAKE GOOD CHOICES.
- ALL PRIORITIES
### RESPONSIBLE USE OF PUBLIC FUNDS
ACCESS for AUSD: S = Success for All
### What I Believe
Every dollar we spend reflects a choice about our priorities.
Every dollar we spend reflects a choice about our priorities. My first priority is protecting the things that directly affect students every day: classroom instruction, legally required services, special education and 504 supports, counselors, safety, and accessibility.
Responsible budgeting also means understanding where money comes from and what it can legally be used for. Restricted funds cannot simply be moved wherever we would prefer to spend them. But the Board still has a responsibility to understand how those funding decisions affect the rest of the district's budget.
### Why It Matters
The Board must understand how restricted funding affects students and the rest of the district’s budget.
A good example is AUSD's significant disproportionality involving Black/African-American students in special education.
AUSD was required to reserve 15% of its federal IDEA Part B funding for Comprehensive Coordinated Early Intervening Services, or CCEIS. Those funds support earlier academic and behavioral intervention in general education.
That is not 15% of the district's General Fund, and it does not eliminate AUSD's obligation to provide legally required IEP services. But when federal special-education dollars are required to be used differently, the Board needs to understand both sides of the equation.
Are the interventions working? Is disproportionality declining? What effect is the funding shift having on the district's ability to meet its other obligations?
Those are oversight questions.
### What I Will Do
Examine spending, demand measurable results, and make financial decisions understandable to the public.
Before looking to classrooms and student services for cuts, I want us examining central-office spending, consultants, vacant administrative positions, travel, contracts without measurable results, and programs that aren't demonstrating sufficient value.
When funding is restricted for a particular purpose, I will ask where the money is going, what intervention it is paying for, how success is being measured, and whether the results justify continuing that approach.
When we're considering major expenditures, I want the public to be able to understand the same information the Board is using to make its decision.
Responsible stewardship isn't just knowing where the money went. It's knowing whether it worked.
### A Current Example: Measure E
Measure E shows why voters need clear promises before an election and visible accountability afterward.
AUSD described Measure E as consolidating and renewing Measures B1 and A while maintaining the same structure and tax rate. The ballot language also allows the Board to establish priorities among the measure’s approved purposes based on available funding.
That does not mean the measure was improper. It means voters deserve a plain-language explanation of what will remain fixed, what may change, and what decisions future Boards will make.
Voters should not have to be lawyers to understand a ballot measure. Available is not the same as clear.
FOLLOW THE MEASURE E REVIEW →
- ALL PRIORITIES
ACCESS for AUSD: A = Access for All
### What I Believe
Accessibility should be built into the way we plan, maintain, and operate our schools.
It should not begin when a student, parent, employee, or community member encounters a barrier.
Accessibility is also more than getting through the front door. Students should be able to participate in their education, move through their campus, use its facilities, and have access to the same programs and opportunities as their peers.
### Why It Matters
Waiting for someone to encounter a barrier places the burden on the person the system should accommodate.
I know what it is like to encounter barriers in public education. I also know what it is like as a parent to discover that a school environment does not fully meet a child's needs.
When accessibility problems are addressed only after someone complains, the burden falls on the very person the system was supposed to accommodate.
That is backwards.
A district responsible for public schools should know where its accessibility barriers are, have a plan for addressing them, and make that information understandable and available to the community.
### What I Will Do
Plan for access from the beginning and hold the district accountable for addressing identified barriers.
As a Board member, I will ask how accessibility is being evaluated when facilities are built, renovated, or maintained. I will push for clear planning, meaningful oversight, and accountability for identified barriers.
I also want families to know where to go when there is a problem and to receive a meaningful response when they raise one.
Most importantly, I want accessibility considered before we spend the money and build the project, not after someone discovers what we missed.
Access should be part of the plan, not an afterthought.
- ALL PRIORITIES
### IEPs, 504s & STUDENT SUPPORT
ACCESS for AUSD: C = Centered on Each Student
### WHAT I BELIEVE
Kids should get their learning accommodations without parents having to fight for them.
IEPs and 504 plans aren't special favors or optional bonuses. They are legal rights that make sure students with disabilities get a fair shot at a great education.
Our goal should be simple: catch needs early, provide the right support immediately, and fix issues before they turn into exhausting legal battles.
### WHY IT MATTERS
I’ve been there, both as a student with an IEP and as a mom fighting for my own kids.
I navigated my own school years with an IEP. Years later, I found myself sitting on the other side of the table, fighting for the IEP and 504 plans my own children need.
I know firsthand how life-changing the right support can be. But I also know how completely exhausting it is to constantly argue with the district just to get the school to follow a plan that's already signed and on paper.
When schools let these problems drag out, everyone loses. Kids fall behind in class, parents lose trust in the system, and stressed-out teachers end up stuck managing conflicts. When problems turn into avoidable legal disputes, money gets spent fighting instead of helping kids.
### WHAT I WILL DO
I will hold the district accountable for delivering the support written into your child’s plan.
A signed document doesn't help a child if it sits in a folder. As a board member, I will hold AUSD accountable and demand to see exactly how they monitor whether IEP and 504 services are actually being delivered every day.
If a service is missing, parents need a clear, direct path to get it fixed immediately. You shouldn't have to hire a lawyer or file a formal complaint just to get a call back.
I will also push the district to track recurring issues across different campuses. If multiple schools are failing to provide the same accommodation, it's a system problem that needs a district-wide fix.
Policies look great on paper, but the real test is whether your child can enter a classroom, participate fully, and thrive.
- ALL PRIORITIES
### FAMILIES & EDUCATORS
DESERVE A VOICE
ACCESS for AUSD: E = Equity in Opportunity
### WHAT I BELIEVE
Real listening happens while there is still time to shape a decision.
Parents and caregivers know their children. Students experience school every day. Educators and staff know what it takes to help them learn.
All deserve a voice in the questions we ask, the options we consider, and the decisions we make.
### WHY IT MATTERS
A busy schedule shouldn't mean your voice doesn't count.
You shouldn't have to sit through hours of meetings or read long reports to understand what is happening at your child’s school.
When you raise a concern, you deserve a real response: what the district knows, what happens next, and who will follow up.
### WHAT I WILL DO
I will listen, ask questions, and explain my votes.
I will meet students, parents and caregivers, educators, and staff at schools and community events, and make it easy to contact me.
Before major decisions, I will push for plain-language explanations and time for the community to help shape the options.
We may not always agree. I will take your concerns seriously and explain how I reached my decision.
- ALL PRIORITIES
### PROTECTING NEIGHBORHOOD SCHOOLS
ACCESS for AUSD: C = Comprehensive Planning
### WHAT I BELIEVE
We shouldn't balance the budget by closing neighborhood schools.
I will not vote to close our neighborhood schools to fix a budget shortfall.
A school is part of a neighborhood’s daily life. Keeping schools open should be a priority as we plan the district’s budget.
### WHY IT MATTERS
The costs of closing a school reach beyond the district’s budget.
Closing a school separates classmates and can mean longer trips, more traffic, and harder schedules for parents and caregivers.
Children may lose the chance to walk or bike to school. Parents may have to juggle new childcare arrangements and siblings at different campuses.
Those are real costs, even when they don’t appear in the district’s budget.
### WHAT I WILL DO
Start with district spending. Give parents and caregivers a voice.
I will push for a close review of administrative costs, consultants, contracts, and vacant office positions to identify savings that protect classrooms.
I will ask for clear budget choices and simple ways to share your views before decisions are made.
You shouldn't have to sit through a long board meeting or read a 100-page report to have a say in your child’s school.
- All Positions
# AI & SCREENS IN SCHOOLS
ACCESS for AUSD: S = Systemic Solutions
### WHAT I BELIEVE
This is the only childhood our kids get.
This is the only childhood our kids get. Schools should give children time to read, write, question, create, and solve problems.
I support a pause on generative AI in student work and staff lesson planning, and an end to routine personal-screen use in classroom instruction. Learning accommodations, assistive technology, and medical needs must remain protected.
Technology companies should have to earn a place in our classrooms.
Sources & supporting information →
### WHY IT MATTERS
Students need intellectual self-defense, not just rules.
Finishing an assignment isn’t the same as learning.
An AI-generated answer doesn’t show what a student understands. AI can also invent facts and repeat biases.
Educator Normand Baillargeon calls the skills needed to recognize manipulation and think for yourself “intellectual self-defense.” Children need opportunities to build those skills through reading, writing, discussion, and hands-on learning.
Sources & supporting information →
### BEFORE AUSD MOVES FORWARD
We need clear evidence, public review, and effective safeguards.
Show us the evidence. Explain the safeguards.
AUSD’s Board Policy 0441 needs clear procedures behind it. Google’s changes to Gemini access show why districts must monitor tools and keep parents and caregivers informed.
Before lifting the pause, AUSD should publicly demonstrate educational benefit, explain privacy protections, and establish how problems will be addressed. The Board should decide through a public, evidence-based vote.
Sources & supporting information →
### WHAT I WILL DO
Students, parents and caregivers, educators, and staff should help shape these decisions.
Give the people affected a real voice.
I will advocate for the pause and the resources teachers need to make these changes.
I support an independent nine-member advisory committee: two students, two parents or caregivers, two educator or staff representatives, and three public-interest experts.
It should meet publicly, disclose conflicts, and publish its own recommendations. The elected Board remains accountable.
Sources & supporting information →

# CELL PHONES IN SCHOOLS
### WHAT I BELIEVE
Teachers should not have to compete with phones for students’ attention.
During instructional time, students should be focused on learning. I support keeping phones off and away.
But off and away does not have to mean inaccessible. Whether a classroom uses backpacks, pouches, a phone hotel, or another system, students should be able to take their phones with them when they leave the classroom while continuing to keep them off and away.
### WHY IT MATTERS
A good policy must account for learning, disability access, and safety.
I support AUSD’s exceptions for students whose IEPs, 504 Plans, or medical needs require access to a personal device. A phone policy should reduce classroom distractions without interfering with the individual supports students need to participate safely and successfully at school.
Lockdowns and other school emergencies are a reality. A student who happens to be outside the classroom when an emergency begins should not be unnecessarily separated from a means of communication.
### WHAT I SUPPORT
Distraction-free classrooms with reasonable access when safety matters.
Taking a phone out of the classroom comes with responsibility. Leaving class is not an opportunity to text, scroll social media, or play games. Students who violate the rules should face appropriate consequences.
We can give teachers the distraction-free classrooms they need while giving students reasonable access to their phones when safety matters.
- All Positions
# LGBTQIA+ STUDENTS & COMMUNITY
ACCESS for AUSD: C = Centered on Each Student
### WHY THIS IS PERSONAL
LGBTQIA+ equality has been part of my life for as long as I can remember.
Before same-sex marriage was legally recognized, my mother, who is bisexual, and her lesbian partner exchanged rings and considered themselves married.
I grew up marching alongside them during a time when LGBTQIA+ people faced far more open public hostility. I remember people spitting on them, screaming at them, and calling them the most derogatory slurs. I watched them keep marching and keep speaking out.
They taught me something I have carried with me ever since: advocacy isn’t just expressing support when it is safe or popular. It means standing up for people even when doing so comes at a personal cost.
Today, that history continues in my own family. I am bisexual. I am the mother of a nonbinary AUSD graduate who had an IEP and a transgender current AUSD student who has a 504 Plan.
### WHAT I BELIEVE
Every student deserves safety, dignity, privacy, and respect.
I have seen firsthand how the policies and practices of a school district can affect a student’s safety, dignity, privacy, and ability to learn.
That’s why I believe AUSD must be unequivocal: discrimination, harassment, bullying, and targeted slurs based on sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression are not acceptable in our schools.
LGBTQIA+ people are our students, parents, teachers, staff members, neighbors, friends, and families. They are part of Alameda.
### RESPONDING APPROPRIATELY
We can respond to students as individuals without excusing discrimination.
Not every incident requires the same response. Age, circumstances, severity, and whether the behavior is repeated all matter.
Sometimes the right response includes education and an opportunity to correct behavior. More serious or repeated conduct may require stronger intervention. But there should never be confusion about the standard itself.
We can respond to students as individuals without making excuses for discrimination.
### WHAT I WILL DO
Policies must protect students in their daily lives, not merely look good on paper.
Students need clear and accessible ways to report what happened. Staff need the training and procedures to respond consistently. Incidents must be documented and followed up on while protecting student privacy.
The Board should receive enough privacy-protected information to ask an important question: Are our policies actually working for students in their daily lives?
A policy that looks good on paper isn’t enough if a student is afraid to report what happened, doesn’t believe anyone will do anything about it, or continues facing the same behavior afterward.
I learned that as a child marching beside my parents. I’ve lived it as a bisexual woman. And I understand the stakes in an entirely different way as the mother of LGBTQIA+ children.
Every student should be able to attend school, participate fully, and learn without having their identity treated as a political issue.
- All Positions
# MUSIC & ARTS IN AUSD
ACCESS for AUSD: E = Equity in Opportunity
### WHAT I BELIEVE
Arts education should not depend on which AUSD school a student attends.
Arts education should be part of an equitable education, not an opportunity determined by which AUSD school a student attends.
I believe equity and accessibility should be built into AUSD’s entire educational plan. We should not have to discover gaps one student, one school, or one complaint at a time. That applies to music and the arts, too.
Equity does not mean every school must have exactly the same program. Different schools and students may need different things. But every student deserves meaningful opportunities to experience music, visual art, theatre, dance, and media arts as part of their education.
### WHY IT MATTERS
The arts can help students discover where they find their voice.
We need to understand what students can actually participate in. What is offered at each school, in which grades, and how often? Can students with disabilities fully participate? Are opportunities built into the school day, or do they depend on fundraising and outside programs?
Every student may not choose to become a musician, artist, actor, dancer, or filmmaker. But every student deserves the opportunity to discover whether the arts are where they find their voice.
### WHAT I WILL DO
I will examine arts access across AUSD and follow the evidence.
I will ask what arts opportunities are available at each school, whether students with disabilities can fully participate, and whether access depends on fundraising, volunteers, outside programs, or families paying for enrichment.
Those questions should guide how we plan, support teachers, and use arts funding, including Proposition 28 funds.
I will listen to students, families, educators, and community advocates while examining district records and state data. I will distinguish what the evidence establishes, what people report, and what still needs clarification.
### ACCOUNTABILITY IN ACTION
I’m beginning a closer look at arts education across AUSD, including school-by-school opportunities and Proposition 28 funding. Create CA’s resources will help guide the questions. AUSD’s records will help us understand what is happening here.
FOLLOW THE WORK →
- All Positions
WHEN COMPLIANCE IS NOT COMMITMENT
ACCESS for AUSD: S = Systemic Solutions
AUSD was required by the state to confront a documented racial disparity. The public deserves to know whether the district changed its culture or merely completed the mandate.
### WHAT HAPPENED
For three consecutive years, Black students were disproportionately identified with certain disabilities.
In 2019–20, the California Department of Education identified AUSD for significant disproportionality involving African American students and certain special-education classifications.
This was not based on one incident or one year of data. Significant disproportionality requires the same racial disparity to appear for three consecutive years.
As a result, AUSD was required to create corrective plans, review its policies and practices, monitor progress, and reserve 15 percent of specified federal special-education funding for Comprehensive Coordinated Early Intervening Services, known as CCEIS.
The state required AUSD to act because the district had not corrected the pattern on its own.
### WHAT THE FINDING REVEALS
A repeated institutional outcome is evidence of an institutional culture.
An institution’s culture is revealed not only by what individuals believe, but by what the system repeatedly permits.
AUSD’s documented, multi-year disproportionality shows that its systems allowed biased judgments and unequal outcomes affecting Black students to persist.
Students were referred, evaluated, classified, supported, and educated through district practices involving professional judgment and human decisions.
Some employees may have recognized and resisted the pattern. But the institution as a whole failed to prevent or correct it before state action became necessary.
That does not mean every educator intended to discriminate. It means AUSD’s culture and systems permitted a harmful racial pattern to continue.
### MANDATE OR MISSION?
The state started the work. Did AUSD make it an institutional priority?
Shamar Edwards, AUSD’s former Senior Director of Equity and African-American, Black, and Multi-Ethnic Achievement, explained the challenge directly:
“The state CCEIS mandate started this work, but I hope we’ll internalize this work, and it comes to be seen as best practice.”
Her words distinguish compliance from commitment. The state could require AUSD to create a plan and redirect funding. It could not guarantee that the district would make the work part of its permanent culture.
The people entrusted with carrying out the work may be deeply committed to its success. But the Board and superintendent are responsible for ensuring that equity becomes an institutional expectation rather than work sustained by a few committed individuals.
The mandate started the work. Governing leadership was responsible for making sure it continued.
### WHAT HAPPENED NEXT?
AUSD’s public page explains the mandate but does not clearly report the outcome.
AUSD’s public significant-disproportionality page still centers on plans and deadlines from 2020. It says progress would be monitored, but it does not clearly tell families what happened next.
The public should not have to search years of Board records or navigate an outside state database to answer basic questions:
- • Did the disparity decline?
- • Did AUSD exit significant-disproportionality status?
- • What referral, assessment, and intervention practices changed?
- • What did AUSD learn from its root-cause review?
- • What safeguards now prevent the pattern from returning?
- • Who currently holds senior responsibility for this work?
If AUSD monitored the results, the public should be able to see them.
### WHO IS ACCOUNTABLE NOW?
The district’s own website does not present a clear chain of responsibility.
Shamar Edwards left AUSD in 2026. The Office of Equity page now identifies Shanti Croom as its coordinator and primary contact, while AUSD’s Leadership Team page still lists Edwards as the district’s Senior Director.
The public website does not clearly identify an interim leader, permanent successor, or current senior official responsible for the district’s significant-disproportionality work.
That does not mean the work has stopped. It means the public cannot readily determine who owns it, how progress is being measured, or who must answer for the results.
A responsibility this important should not disappear into an outdated directory.
### WHY ACCESS MATTERS
Equity must be built into the district’s culture, not added after harm is documented.
ACCESS means examining the entire system that shapes a student’s education. It means questioning accepted practices, listening to affected families, measuring unequal outcomes, and acting before the state forces the district to respond.
As a Board member, I will ask what changed, what the evidence shows, who is accountable, and how the district will prevent the same pattern from returning.
Compliance means completing the required plan. Commitment means making the results public, continuing the work after the mandate ends, and changing the culture that allowed the harm to occur.
Black students should not have to experience years of unequal outcomes before AUSD decides equity is urgent.
- BACK

### WHY I'M ASKING
Community voices should lead to questions, evidence, and action.

Alameda arts advocate Katherine Park raised questions with me about access to music and arts across our schools. She also brought Create CA’s research and resources to my attention. Her work deserves support, and I intend to help move it forward.

I’m beginning a school-by-school look at music, visual art, theatre, dance, and media arts across AUSD.

We need to understand what students gain from Proposition 28 funding.

MEASURE E: PROMISES, PRIORITIES & PUBLIC TRUST
ACCESS for AUSD: C = Comprehensive Planning
Ballot measures are a promise to the public.
When AUSD asks voters to approve a tax, people should know what the money will support. They should also know what can change, who will make those choices, and how the public can check the results.
Measure E provides important local funding for Alameda schools. AUSD said it would renew and combine Measures B1 and A without raising the tax rate.
I am comparing what voters were told, what the measure allows, what the Board decided, and how the money is being spent.
### What Voters Were Told
AUSD told voters Measure E would renew and combine two existing taxes without raising the tax rate.
AUSD told voters that Measure E would combine, replace, and renew Measures B1 and A. The District said the tax structure and rate would stay the same.
The District also said the money would continue to support academic programs, employee pay, help for struggling students, arts, sports, and neighborhood schools.
Those statements shaped what voters thought they were approving.
### What Voters Approved
Measure E lists how the money may be used, but the Board decides which approved needs come first.
The full Measure E text lists the purposes for which the money may be spent. It also says spending will follow priorities set by the Board and depend on available funds.
That does not allow the Board to spend the money on anything it wants. The money must stay within the purposes voters approved.
However, the Board can decide which of those approved needs come first.
Measure E also requires a separate account, public financial reports, a yearly audit, and an advisory oversight committee. The Board decides the committee’s size, structure, and duties.
That gives the Board both power and responsibility. It must set priorities and explain those choices clearly.
### Why the Difference Matters
“Renew and combine” sounds like the old promises will continue. Voters also need to know what could change.
When voters heard that Measure E would renew and combine Measures B1 and A, what did they believe would stay the same?
Did they think only the tax rate and structure would remain the same? Did they also expect the earlier funding promises and oversight rules to continue?
I do not know the answers yet. They require a careful comparison of all three measures and the information given to voters.
A document can be available to the public and still be difficult to understand.
Available is not the same as clear.
### What I’m Checking
I am comparing what voters were told with what the measure says and how the money is being used.
I am reviewing:
- The original text of Measures B1, A, and E
- The public information used to explain Measure E
- The spending plans and Board decisions involving Measure E
- The oversight committee’s structure, duties, and reports
- Measure E revenue and spending
- Whether the public can easily compare what voters were promised with what the money delivered
Records requests help us understand what happened. They do not prove that anyone did something wrong.
### Where the Work Stands
This review is beginning, and I have not reached any conclusions.
Measure E took effect on July 1, 2025.
I have not completed a side-by-side comparison of Measures B1, A, and E. I also have not reviewed every spending report or Board decision involving Measure E.
As I review the records, I will separate what the documents show, what the District told voters, what the spending reports show, and what still needs an answer.
I will share evidence that supports the District’s decisions, evidence that raises questions, and information that remains unclear.
### My Standard for Accountability
Clear promises before the vote. Visible results afterward.
Voters should not need a law degree to understand a ballot measure.
Before an election, the District should clearly explain what will stay the same, what may change, and what choices future Boards will make.
After the election, the public should be able to follow those choices and see what the money accomplished.
Accountability is not hostility. It means checking whether public promises, public decisions, and public results match.

AI & SCREENS: SOURCES BEHIND MY POSITION
These references are grouped by the sections they inform. Research findings, district documents, reporting, and my policy proposals serve different purposes.Sources are included to help readers examine the evidence, including findings that complicate my position.
## AI & Screens: Sources and Supporting Information
### WHAT I BELIEVE
Reading on paper and screens: Delgado and colleagues (2018) ↗
A meta-analysis found a small average comprehension advantage for paper, especially for informational texts and under time pressure. It does not establish that every screen activity is harmful.
Excessive screen time and child development (2023 review) ↗
Reviews concerns about excessive exposure, media multitasking, and development. It also discusses benefits of some uses. This is background evidence, not a trial of a school screen ban.
The PANIC study: screen time and cognition (2026) ↗
This eight-year observational study found an association between greater reported screen time and better overall cognitive performance. It did not establish causation or directly test critical thinking. This finding is included because the evidence is mixed.
### WHY IT MATTERS
Normand Baillargeon: A Short Course in Intellectual Self-Defense ↗
The publisher describes Baillargeon’s work on evaluating information and recognizing manipulation. It informs the intellectual self-defense principle; it is not an experimental study of classroom AI.
Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (2025) ↗
In a high-school math experiment, general-purpose AI assistance improved practice performance but reduced subsequent unaided exam performance. A safeguarded tutor showed no statistically detectable difference from the no-AI group on that exam. The study examined short-term learning in one setting.
Patricia Greenfield: Technology and Informal Education (2009) ↗
This research-based perspective discusses differences between visual skills and reflective thought. It recommends a balanced media diet with ample reading and reflection; it is not a modern classroom screen-ban trial.
AI-assisted lesson preparation: EEF trial ↗
Teachers using ChatGPT with guidance spent less time preparing selected science lessons, with no apparent reduction in reviewed resource quality. The trial did not establish improved student learning. It is relevant evidence when examining staff use.
### BEFORE AUSD MOVES FORWARD
AUSD AI implementation presentation ↗
District agenda materials concerning AI implementation. These document the district’s approach, rather than independently establish learning benefits.
AUSD review of Board Policy 0441 ↗
District agenda materials concerning its AI policy. Read alongside implementation procedures and subsequent Board actions.
AUSD online applications and student privacy ↗
District information about online applications and student privacy.
Common Sense Media: Google’s Gemini changes ↗
Reporting and analysis of a default-on change affecting schools that had already enabled certain Gemini services. It supports questions about vendor changes and school notice; it does not establish that the same change occurred in AUSD.
Education Week: schools and Gemini access ↗
Additional reporting linked from the campaign’s earlier position page. Access may require a subscription.
Google: communicating with parents and guardians ↗
Google’s guidance on service access, communication, and consent. This is the vendor’s description of its arrangements, not an independent evaluation of educational value.
### WHAT I WILL DO
The moratorium, restrictions on routine personal-screen instruction, and nine-member independent advisory committee are my policy proposals. The committee’s size, membership, and independence provisions are recommendations for AUSD, not conclusions dictated by a research study.
The evidence above would inform public review. Any decision to permit use should identify its educational purpose, supporting evidence, safeguards, and conditions for reconsideration.
